chapter: Los Angeles 1947-48, Rock Island and bebop in New York
title: Scoops Carey, the windy alto who became a lawyer
summary: Carey's big breaths unsettled saxophone sections; he left music, practiced law and passed for white.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: They had a wonderful alto player, first alto man, in that group. He was an ex alumni from Roy Eldridge's band, when he had the Three Deuces in Chicago. Scoops Carey.
Yeah. I've heard a lot about him.

But he could take -- he was so windy, he could take such large breaths that the rest of the saxophone section couldn't phrase with him, see, because he would hold out until he would turn red in the face, you know, to get a phrase through, and they couldn't follow him. So he couldn't keep a job because of this. He was just too good, you know. So he was so good that he quit playing music and went back to law school for a year and got his shingle, and he put it out in the Loop. He started passing. He was fair-skinned and his hair was all right, so they thought he was white. And he was coming into the Capital Lounge where Roy and I were working, and he would hold his head down. We'd laugh.
